explain.say: Turn on your kitchen tap and look at the sink. The water spreads in a thin, fast sheet, then suddenly piles up into a ring of deeper, slower water. That ring is a hydraulic jump, and the same thing roars at the foot of every big dam spillway. On the board, water half a metre deep races in at six metres per second.

explain.say: First check the Froude number before the jump: six over the square root of nine point eight one times zero point five, about two point seven. That is supercritical, faster than surface waves can travel. A fast, shallow flow like this cannot carry on if the channel downstream is deeper. Something has to give. What do you think happens?

marks.label: Before: 0.5 m
marks.ask: Why does a hydraulic jump happen?

marks.label: After: 1.68 m
marks.ask: How do you calculate the depth after a hydraulic jump?

explain.say: It jumps! The depth after the jump comes from momentum: the new depth is half the old depth times the square root of one plus eight times the Froude number squared, minus one. That gives one point six eight metres, more than three times deeper, now moving at only one point seven eight metres per second.

explain.say: Where did the energy go? Before the jump the flow carried two point three three metres of head; after it, one point eight four. About a fifth, zero point four nine metres, is churned into turbulence and finally heat in the swirling roller. At a dam, that is exactly the jump's job: to destroy energy safely.

explain.say: Engineers build stilling basins, concrete aprons with blocks and an end sill, to hold the jump in place so the fast water cannot scour the riverbed. Wonderful work! Challenge: in your sink, does the ring move outward or inward when you turn the tap up?

faq.a: A hydraulic jump is a sudden rise in water level where fast, shallow supercritical flow changes to slow, deep subcritical flow, with a turbulent roller that dissipates energy.

faq.q: How do you calculate the depth after a hydraulic jump?
faq.a: Use the sequent depth equation from momentum: y2 over y1 equals a half times the square root of 1 plus 8 Fr1 squared, minus 1. For 0.5 metres at Froude 2.71, y2 is about 1.68 metres.

faq.q: How much energy is lost in a hydraulic jump?
faq.a: In a rectangular channel the head lost is (y2 minus y1) cubed over 4 y1 y2. Here that is about 0.49 metres, roughly a fifth of the incoming energy.
A stilling basin is a concrete apron at the foot of a spillway or sluice, often with chute blocks, baffle blocks and an end sill, that forces a hydraulic jump to form there and protects the riverbed.
asks: How does a stilling basin work?

faq.q: Why does a hydraulic jump happen?
faq.a: Supercritical flow cannot gradually slow down to meet a deeper subcritical flow downstream. Instead it changes abruptly, conserving momentum but losing energy, in a jump.

facts: The sequent depth ratio is y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1), from conservation of momentum.
The head lost in a hydraulic jump in a rectangular channel is (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂).

quiz.say: Before a jump the depth is 0.4 metres and the Froude number is 3. What is the depth after the jump? The square root of 73 is about 8.54.
quiz.show: Before a jump y₁ = 0.4 m and Fr₁ = 3. Depth after the jump (√73 ≈ 8.54)?

wrong.1: That just multiplies the depth by the Froude number.
wrong.2: That forgets to subtract 1 and halve.

quiz.say: A hydraulic jump can only form when the incoming flow is…
quiz.show: A hydraulic jump can only form when the incoming flow is…
quiz.why: A jump changes supercritical flow, Froude above 1, into subcritical flow.

wrong.0: Subcritical flow is what comes out of a jump.
wrong.1: At exactly Froude 1 there is no jump, just an unsteady surface.
